mainTopic: Animal reproduction in a ברייתא: live birth versus eggs, timing of birth, the יום טוב egg, mating and pregnancy lengths, and the snake's seven years
overview: This amud continues a ברייתא about how creatures reproduce. It first says the דולפנין (sea creatures) reproduce like people. It then gives a sign for which animals give live birth and which lay eggs. The goose case forces the גמרא to correct that sign: what counts is whether the male organ is external, not the testicles. Next the ברייתא says animals give birth at the same time of day they mate. That rule is used to permit an egg found before daylight on יום טוב, together with רבי יוחנן's rule that an egg counts as laid once most of it has come out. The ברייתא then teaches that two species can breed together only if they mate the same way and carry their young for the same length of time. It lists the ways of mating and the pregnancy lengths of many animals, each matched to a tree. רב יהודה derives the snake's seven-year pregnancy from its curse in בראשית using a one-to-seven ratio. The גמרא then challenges this with a one-to-three ratio that would give nine years, and the discussion continues on the next amud.

steps.title: The דולפנין reproduce like humans
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא states that the דולפנין reproduce the way people do.
steps.simpleTranslation: The dulfanin reproduce like people.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא, which is listing how different creatures reproduce, says that a sea creature called דולפנין reproduces like humans do.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This is part of a longer ברייתא about reproduction in the animal world. The point is that even though the דולפנין live in the sea, they reproduce the way humans do rather than the way fish do.

keyTerms.meaning: A kind of sea creature; the גמרא will explain the word next

phrases.english: The dulfanin reproduce
like people.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the ברייתא on reproduction from the previous part of the daf.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The דולפנין reproduce in the way humans do.

steps.title: What are דולפנין?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what creature the word דולפנין refers to.
steps.simpleTranslation: What are dulfanin?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks a simple vocabulary question: what is a דולפנין? This sets up the answer in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This is not an attack on the ברייתא. The word is unusual, so the גמרא wants to know which creature it means.

phrases.english: What are dulfanin?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for the meaning of a word used in Step 1.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The identity of the creature called דולפנין.

steps.title: רב יהודה: They are 'sons of the sea'
steps.stepSummary: רב יהודה explains that דולפנין are the creatures called בני ימא.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב יהודה says: They are 'sons of the sea.'
steps.whatsHappening: רב יהודה answers the question: דולפנין are the creatures known as בני ימא, 'sons of the sea.'
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב יהודה matches the unusual word to a name people already knew. This makes clear that the ברייתא is talking about a sea creature.

keyTerms.meaning: 'Sons of the sea'; the name for these sea creatures

phrases.english: Rav Yehuda says:
Sons of the sea.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of Step 2.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: דולפנין are the creatures called בני ימא.

steps.title: The ברייתא's sign: where the male's testicles are
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא gives a sign: external testicles means the species gives birth to live young, and internal testicles means it lays eggs.
steps.simpleTranslation: Any animal whose testicles are on the outside gives birth, and any whose testicles are inside lays eggs.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא continues with a general rule. Look at the male: if his testicles are external, the species gives birth to live young; if they are internal, it lays eggs.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This is a simple physical sign for sorting creatures into two groups: those that give live birth and those that lay eggs. The next step will test whether this sign really works.

keyTerms.meaning: Here, testicles. The same word also means eggs.

steps.confusionAlert: The word ביצים is used in two different senses in this sugya. In 'ביציו מבחוץ' it means testicles. In 'מטיל ביצים' it means eggs. Keep them apart, or the rule will sound like nonsense.

phrases.english: Any whose testicles are on the outside
gives birth (to live young),
and any whose (testicles) are inside
lays eggs.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Returns to the ברייתא after the side question about the word דולפנין.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Male testicles external means the species gives live birth; male testicles internal means it lays eggs.

steps.title: Challenge from the two kinds of geese
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges the sign from שמואל's ruling. As אביי explains it, a wild goose has external testicles and a domestic goose has internal ones, yet both lay eggs.
steps.simpleTranslation: Is that so? But שמואל said that a goose and a wild goose are כלאים with each other. We asked why, and אביי answered: one has external testicles and the other has internal testicles. Yet both lay eggs!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא attacks the ברייתא's sign. It brings an example where a bird has external testicles but still lays eggs.
steps.deeperAnalysis: שמואל ruled that a domestic goose and a wild goose are כלאים, meaning they are different species. אביי explained that this is because their testicles are in different places. Yet both kinds of geese lay eggs, so external testicles cannot be the sign of live birth.

keyTerms.meaning: 'And we discussed it'; brings up an earlier discussion

phrases.english: Is that so?
But didn't Shmuel say:
A (domestic) goose and a wild goose
are diverse kinds with each other,
phrases.notes: He means they count as two different species, so they may not be mated together.

phrases.english: and we discussed it: What is the reason?
phrases.notes: They look so alike, so why would they count as different species?

phrases.english: Abaye said:
This one's testicles are external,
and that one's testicles are internal,
and both of them lay eggs!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the sign given in Step 4.
steps.kashyaTarget: The ברייתא's rule that external testicles means live birth.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The wild goose has external testicles, as אביי says when explaining שמואל, yet it lays eggs. That is a counterexample to the rule.

steps.title: Corrected sign: the male organ, not the testicles
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא rereads the ברייתא. The sign is whether the male reproductive organ is external or internal, not where the testicles are.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, any animal whose male organ is external gives birth, and any whose organ is internal lays eggs.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge by rereading the ברייתא. The sign depends on where the male organ is, not where the testicles are.
steps.deeperAnalysis: With this reading, the goose case is no longer a problem. A wild goose may have external testicles, but its male organ is internal, so it lays eggs. The ברייתא stands; only its sign is adjusted.
steps.whatToRemember: The final sign is the male organ. If it is external, the species gives birth to live young. If it is internal, the species lays eggs. Where the testicles are does not decide it, as the wild goose shows.

phrases.english: Rather, any whose male organ is external
gives birth (to live young),
(if its organ is) internal, it lays eggs.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the קשיא of Step 5 by rereading the ברייתא from Step 4.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The sign was the location of the testicles.
steps.terutzMaskana: The sign is the location of the male organ. External means live birth; internal means laying eggs.

steps.title: Animals give birth at the same time of day they mate
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא states that a species gives birth at the time of day it mates: by day, by night, or both.
steps.simpleTranslation: Any species that mates during the day gives birth during the day. One that mates at night gives birth at night. One that mates both by day and by night gives birth both by day and by night.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא that gave the sign for live birth versus egg-laying keeps going and gives another rule about animals: the timing of birth matches the timing of mating.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This is a new rule, separate from the earlier sign about live birth versus eggs. It splits all creatures into three groups: day-only, night-only, and both. The גמרא will soon fill in examples and show why this matters in הלכה.

keyTerms.meaning: Gives birth (for birds, this means lays eggs)
Both by day and by night

phrases.english: Any species whose mating is in the daytime gives birth in the daytime,
one that mates at night gives birth at night,

phrases.aramaic: כֹּל שֶׁתַּשְׁמִישׁוֹ בֵּין בַּיּוֹם בֵּין בַּלַּיְלָה —
phrases.english: any species whose mating is both in the daytime and at night
gives birth both in the daytime and at night.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the same ברייתא that gave the testicle and organ sign, now adding a new rule about timing.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A species gives birth at the same time of day that it mates: day, night, or both.

steps.title: Examples: chicken, bat, and human
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא names an example for each group: a chicken mates and lays by day, a bat by night, and a human both.
steps.simpleTranslation: Mating by day and giving birth by day is the chicken. By night and giving birth by night is the bat. Both by day and by night is a human and any creature like him.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains the ברייתא's three groups by giving a real creature for each one.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The rule now has concrete examples. The chicken example is the important one: a chicken lays its eggs only during the day. The very next steps build on that fact.

phrases.english: Mating by day, giving birth by day: a chicken,
by night, giving birth by night: a bat,
mating both by day and by night,
giving birth both by day and by night:
a human and anything similar to him.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives a real example for each of the three groups in the ברייתא.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A chicken mates and lays only by day, a bat only by night, and humans at both times.

steps.title: What practical difference does this make?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks why it matters in הלכה when an animal gives birth.
steps.simpleTranslation: What difference does it make?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks what this piece of nature has to do with הלכה. This question sets up the next step, which gives the answer.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The גמרא wants to know why a ברייתא would teach this fact at all. It is looking for a case where knowing that chickens lay only by day changes a ruling.

keyTerms.meaning: What practical difference does it make?

phrases.english: For what does it make a difference?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for the practical use of the rule and examples just given.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: A halachic case where knowing whether an animal gives birth by day or by night makes a difference.

steps.title: An egg found early on יום טוב morning is permitted
steps.stepSummary: רב מרי בריה דרב כהנא rules that an egg found before daylight on יום טוב is permitted. A chicken does not lay at night, so it must have been laid before יום טוב and he just missed it.
steps.simpleTranslation: This matters for the ruling of רב מרי בריה דרב כהנא. He said: if someone checked a chicken's nest on ערב יום טוב and found no egg, then got up early the next morning and found an egg, it is permitted to eat on יום טוב. We say he simply did not check carefully.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the question: the 'day only' rule for chickens is the basis of רב מרי's ruling about an egg found early on יום טוב.
steps.deeperAnalysis: An egg laid on יום טוב is forbidden to eat that day. Here the egg was found very early, before daylight. Since chickens lay only by day, it could not have been laid during the night, so it must have been laid on ערב יום טוב. The empty nest the day before is explained away: he did not check well.
steps.confusionAlert: Do not think the egg is permitted only because he 'didn't check well.' The real reason is that chickens don't lay at night. That fact forces us to say the egg was already there, so his check must have missed it.

phrases.english: For the ruling of רב מרי, son of רב כהנא,

phrases.aramaic: דְּאָמַר רַב מָרִי בְּרֵיהּ דְּרַב כָּהֲנָא:
phrases.english: as רב מרי, son of רב כהנא, said:

phrases.aramaic: בָּדַק בְּקִינָּה שֶׁל תַּרְנְגוֹלִין מֵעֶרֶב יוֹם טוֹב
phrases.english: If one checked a chickens' nest on the eve of the festival
and did not find an egg in it,
and the next day he got up early and found an egg in it,
phrases.notes: 'Got up early' means before daylight, so a chicken could not have laid it that morning.

phrases.english: it is permitted to eat on the festival,
for we say: he did not check carefully.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 9 by giving a ruling that depends on chickens laying only by day.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The difference is רב מרי's ruling: an egg found before daylight on יום טוב must have been laid on ערב יום טוב, so it is permitted.
steps.whyThisMatters: It shows how a fact about nature (chickens lay only by day) decides a real question about eating on יום טוב.

steps.title: But he did check carefully
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא objects: the case says he checked the nest, so how can we just say he missed the egg?
steps.simpleTranslation: But he did check carefully!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the explanation that the person 'did not check well,' because the case says he checked.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ruling depended on saying the egg was there all along and was missed. But if the check was a good one, the egg really was not in the nest on ערב יום טוב. Then where did it come from, if chickens don't lay at night?

phrases.english: But he did check carefully!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the assumption in step 10 that the check was not careful.
steps.kashyaTarget: The explanation 'he did not check carefully' in רב מרי's ruling.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The case says he checked and found nothing, so we cannot just say he missed the egg. A careful check means the egg was not there before יום טוב.

steps.title: The egg partly came out and went back in, as רבי יוחנן rules
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that most of the egg came out on ערב יום טוב and then went back inside the hen. Following רבי יוחנן, that egg counts as already laid before יום טוב and is permitted.
steps.simpleTranslation: Say that most of the egg came out and went back in. This follows רבי יוחנן, who said: an egg that mostly came out on ערב יום טוב and then went back in is permitted to eat on יום טוב.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא defends רב מרי's ruling. Even if the check was careful, the egg can count as laid before יום טוב.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The new picture: on ערב יום טוב most of the egg came out of the hen and slipped back in, so the nest looked empty. רבי יוחנן rules that once most of an egg has come out, it counts as laid. So the egg found in the morning was really 'laid' before יום טוב, and the ruling stands.
steps.whatToRemember: Chickens lay only by day, so an egg found before daylight on יום טוב is permitted. If the nest was really empty the day before, we say most of the egg came out on ערב יום טוב and went back in, and רבי יוחנן rules that this counts as already laid.

phrases.english: Say: it was a case where most of it came out and went back in,
phrases.notes: 'It' is the egg: most of it came out of the hen on ערב יום טוב and slipped back inside, so the nest looked empty.

phrases.english: and this follows רבי יוחנן, as רבי יוחנן said:

phrases.aramaic: בֵּיצָה שֶׁיָּצְתָה רוּבָּהּ מֵעֶרֶב יוֹם טוֹב
phrases.english: an egg most of which came out on the eve of the festival
and then went back in is permitted to eat on the festival.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 11 by changing how we picture the case, using רבי יוחנן's rule.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Reframing the case plus support from another אמורא's ruling
steps.terutzHavaAmina: If he checked carefully and found nothing, the egg must have been laid on יום טוב itself and should be forbidden.
steps.terutzMaskana: Most of the egg came out on ערב יום טוב and went back in. By רבי יוחנן's rule it already counts as laid, so it is permitted.
steps.whyThisMatters: It shows the rule that 'most of it came out' counts as fully out, which decides when an egg is considered born.

steps.title: Same mating and pregnancy means two species can breed together
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא states a rule: two different species that mate the same way and carry their young for the same time can have offspring together and can nurse each other's young.
steps.simpleTranslation: Any animals whose way of mating and length of pregnancy are the same can have babies together and can raise each other's young.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא continues with a new rule about animals of different species. If they mate the same way and have the same pregnancy length, they can breed together and nurse each other's babies.
steps.deeperAnalysis: There are two conditions here, and both are needed: the same way of mating (תשמיש) and the same pregnancy length (עיבור). The next line explains the first condition, the way of mating.

keyTerms.meaning: Pregnancy, how long the animal carries its young
Raise, here meaning nurse the young
Each other's, one from the other

phrases.english: Any whose mating and pregnancy are the same
can have young and raise each other's young.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Returns to the ברייתא about animal nature after the side discussion of the יום טוב egg.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Two species can breed together and nurse each other's young only if they share the same way of mating and the same pregnancy length.

steps.title: Most creatures mate face-to-back, three mate face-to-face
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא explains the ways of mating: nearly all creatures mate with the male behind the female, but fish, humans, and snakes mate face-to-face.
steps.simpleTranslation: All creatures mate with the face of one toward the back of the other's neck, except three that mate face-to-face: fish, humans, and snakes.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא now explains the first condition from the last step, the way of mating. It gives the general rule and three exceptions.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The normal way is face-to-back, meaning the male comes from behind. Fish, people, and snakes are the exceptions. This sets up the גמרא's question about why these three are different.

keyTerms.meaning: Face opposite the back of the neck, the male behind the female

phrases.english: All mate face opposite the back of the neck,
except for three
that mate face-to-face,
and these are: fish, human, and snake.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains the first condition, the way of mating, from step 13.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Creatures mate face-to-back, except fish, humans, and snakes, which mate face-to-face.

steps.title: Why are these three different?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what is special about fish, humans, and snakes that they mate face-to-face.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is different about these three?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks a simple question: why do only these three creatures mate face-to-face? It is setting up the answer in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This is not an attack on the ברייתא. The גמרא wants a reason that ties together three very different creatures: a fish, a person, and a snake.

phrases.english: And what is different about these three?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for the reason behind the three exceptions in step 14.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Why fish, humans, and snakes alone mate face-to-face.

steps.title: Because the שכינה spoke with them
steps.stepSummary: רב דימי reports that in ארץ ישראל they explain that these three are different because the שכינה spoke with them.
steps.simpleTranslation: When רב דימי came, he said that in the West they say: because the Divine Presence spoke with them.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the question. רב דימי brings the explanation from ארץ ישראל: these three are special because the שכינה spoke with them.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The link between the three is not physical. Each one was spoken to by the שכינה, and that special status is shown in the face-to-face way they mate.

keyTerms.meaning: When he came, used for a rabbi arriving from ארץ ישראל to Bavel

phrases.english: When רב דימי came,
they say in the West:
phrases.notes: "The West" means ארץ ישראל, which is west of בבל.

phrases.english: since the Divine Presence spoke with them.

steps.triggerLanguage: כִּי אֲתָא רַב דִּימִי אָמְרִי בְּמַעְרְבָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question in step 15.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: These three are different because the שכינה spoke with them.

steps.title: A camel mates back-to-back
steps.stepSummary: A תנא adds another unusual case: camels mate back-to-back.
steps.simpleTranslation: It was taught: a camel mates back-to-back.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא adds one more unusual way of mating, from a ברייתא. Camels mate back-to-back.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This adds to the list from step 14. Besides face-to-back and face-to-face, there is a third way, which camels use.

phrases.english: It was taught: A camel
back to back.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds another way of mating to the list in step 14.

steps.title: How long animals carry their young, with matching trees
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא lists how long several animals carry their young and pairs each with a tree or plant that takes the same time to ripen.
steps.simpleTranslation: The Rabbis taught: a chicken takes twenty-one days, and the matching tree is the almond. A dog takes fifty days, and the matching tree is the fig. A cat takes fifty-two days, and the matching tree is the mulberry. A pig takes sixty days, and the matching tree is the apple. A fox and all kinds of creeping creatures take six months, and the matching plant is grain.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא about the second condition from step 13, pregnancy length. It lists how long each animal takes to give birth and matches it to a tree that takes the same time to ripen.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The step 13 rule needed pregnancy lengths, and here we get a list of them. Each animal is paired with a plant that ripens in the same number of days, from the 21-day chicken to the six-month fox.

keyTerms.meaning: The matching tree, the one that takes the same time

steps.whatToRemember: Two species can breed together only if they mate the same way and carry their young the same length of time. The גמרא lists the ways of mating (face-to-back, face-to-face, back-to-back) and the pregnancy lengths, each matched to a tree or plant.

phrases.english: The Rabbis taught:
A chicken hatches after twenty-one days,
and its match among trees is the almond,
a dog gives birth after fifty days,
and its match among trees is the fig,
a cat gives birth after fifty-two days,
and its match among trees is the mulberry,
a pig gives birth after sixty days,
its match among trees is the apple,

phrases.aramaic: שׁוּעָל וְכׇל מִינֵי שְׁרָצִים — שִׁשָּׁה חֳדָשִׁים,
phrases.english: a fox and all kinds of creeping creatures give birth after six months,
and their match among trees is grain.

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּנוּ רַבָּנַן: תַּרְנְגוֹלֶת — לְעֶשְׂרִים וְאֶחָד יוֹם
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from the way of mating to the second condition from step 13, pregnancy length.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Chicken 21 days (almond), dog 50 (fig), cat 52 (mulberry), pig 60 (apple), fox and creeping creatures six months (grain).

steps.title: More animals and their matching trees
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא continues its list. Small kosher animals match the grapevine, large non-kosher animals match the date palm, large kosher animals match the olive, and a group of wild animals matches the white fig.
steps.simpleTranslation: Small kosher animals give birth after five months, and the grapevine matches them. Large non-kosher animals give birth after twelve months, and the date palm matches them. Large kosher animals give birth after nine months, and the olive matches them. The wolf, lion, bear, leopard, ברדלס, elephant, monkey and long-tailed ape give birth after three years, and the white fig matches them.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא from step 18 keeps going with more animals, giving how long each carries its young and the tree that matches it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Each line has the same pattern: a type of animal, its pregnancy length, and then a tree that takes the same time to ripen. The animals are sorted by size (small or large) and by kosher status (טהורה or טמאה).

keyTerms.meaning: Small livestock, like sheep and goats
Large livestock, like cows, donkeys and camels
And the tree that matches them
White figs, a kind of fig tree

phrases.english: Small kosher livestock — give birth after five months,
and the tree that matches them is the grapevine.

phrases.aramaic: בְּהֵמָה גַּסָּה טְמֵאָה — לִשְׁנֵים עָשָׂר חוֹדֶשׁ,
phrases.english: Large non-kosher livestock — after twelve months,
and the tree that matches it is the date palm.
Kosher (large livestock) — after nine months,
and the tree that matches it is the olive.
The wolf, the lion, the bear, the leopard,

phrases.aramaic: וְהַבַּרְדְּלָס וְהַפִּיל וְהַקּוֹף וְהַקִּיפוֹף — לְשָׁלֹשׁ שָׁנִים,
phrases.english: the ברדלס, the elephant, the monkey and the long-tailed ape — after three years,
phrases.notes: ברדלס is a wild animal. People explain it in different ways, often as a hyena-like creature.

phrases.english: and the tree that matches them is the white fig.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the same ברייתא list begun in step 18.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Each animal group's pregnancy length matches the ripening time of a certain tree.

steps.title: The viper and the carob tree
steps.stepSummary: The אפעה (viper) carries for seventy years and matches the carob tree. The carob takes seventy years from planting to full fruit, and its fruit takes three years to form.
steps.simpleTranslation: A viper gives birth after seventy years, and the carob tree matches it. This carob takes seventy years from planting until its fruit is fully ripe, and its 'pregnancy' (the time for its fruit to form) is three years.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא gives an extreme case: the viper, whose pregnancy lasts seventy years, matched with the slow-growing carob.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא explains why the carob fits. It takes seventy years from planting until it fully produces. It also notes that each crop of fruit takes three years to develop, which it calls the tree's 'pregnancy.'

keyTerms.meaning: A viper, a kind of poisonous snake
Its days of pregnancy, here meaning the time it takes its fruit to form

phrases.english: A viper — after seventy years,
and the tree that matches it is the carob.
This carob, from the time it is planted

phrases.aramaic: עַד שְׁעַת גְּמַר פֵּירוֹתָיו — שִׁבְעִים שָׁנָה,
phrases.english: until its fruit is fully ripe — is seventy years,
and its 'pregnancy' lasts three years.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the list with the longest example.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Viper: seventy years, matched with the carob.

steps.title: The snake has no matching tree
steps.stepSummary: The נחש carries for seven years, and no tree matches that wicked creature. Some say the מוכססים tree does match it.
steps.simpleTranslation: A snake gives birth after seven years, and for that wicked one we have found no partner among the trees. Some say: the מוכססים tree matches it.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא ends its list with the נחש. It says no tree matches it, though one opinion names the מוכססים.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The נחש is called 'wicked' because of its part in the sin of אדם and חוה, and it is left without a matching tree. The 'some say' opinion disagrees and offers the מוכססים as a tree that takes seven years. This seven-year claim is what the גמרא will question next.

keyTerms.meaning: A partner, here meaning a matching tree
A type of tree said to take seven years to produce

phrases.english: A snake — after seven years,
and for that wicked one we have not found a partner.
phrases.notes: 'That wicked one' is the snake from גן עדן. No tree matches its seven years.

phrases.english: And some say: מוכססים.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Final item of the ברייתא's list.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The snake carries for seven years. Either no tree matches it, or the מוכססים does.

steps.title: Where do we know the snake's seven years from?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks for the source of the claim that the נחש carries for seven years.
steps.simpleTranslation: From where do we know these things?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks for a source for the snake's seven-year pregnancy. This question sets up the answer that comes next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Of all the numbers in the list, the seven years for the נחש is the one the גמרא wants backed up. The answer will come from a פסוק.

keyTerms.meaning: From where do we know these things? (asking for a source)

phrases.english: From where are these matters known?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for the source of the seven-year figure in step 21.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The source for the snake's seven-year pregnancy.

steps.title: The source is the curse of the snake
steps.stepSummary: רב יהודה, quoting רב (some say it was in the name of רבי יהושע בן חנניא), brings the פסוק 'Cursed are you more than all the animals and all the beasts of the field.'
steps.simpleTranslation: רב יהודה said in the name of רב, and some say it goes back to רבי יהושע בן חנניא: As it says, 'Cursed are you more than all the animals and more than all the beasts of the field.'
steps.whatsHappening: רב יהודה answers by quoting the curse הקב"ה gave the נחש in גן עדן.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The curse is read as saying the נחש's pregnancy will be longer than every other animal's. The פסוק names two groups, tame animals (בהמה) and wild animals (חיה), and the next step will ask why both are needed.

keyTerms.meaning: And some carried it back to the name of (traced the teaching to an earlier sage)

phrases.english: רב יהודה said that רב said,

phrases.aramaic: וּמָטוּ בָּהּ מִשּׁוּם דְּרַבִּי יְהוֹשֻׁעַ בֶּן חֲנַנְיָא,
phrases.english: and some traced it back to the name of רבי יהושע בן חנניא,
as it says: 'Cursed are you more than all the animals
phrases.notes: This is בראשית 3:14, the snake's punishment after the sin in the Garden.

phrases.english: and more than all the beasts of the field.'

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 22 with a פסוק.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The curse of the snake in בראשית 3:14.

steps.title: Why mention the wild animals at all?
steps.stepSummary: If the נחש was cursed more than the tame animals, it is obviously cursed more than the wild animals. So why does the פסוק add them?
steps.simpleTranslation: If it was cursed more than the tame animals, isn't it all the more so cursed more than the wild animals?
steps.whatsHappening: As part of his derivation, רב יהודה points out a difficulty in the wording of the פסוק: the mention of wild animals seems extra.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The shortest tame-animal pregnancy (a goat, five months) is already longer than the shortest wild-animal pregnancy (a cat, about 52 days). So if the snake's pregnancy is longer than the tame animals', it seems obvious it is longer than the wild animals' too. That makes 'beasts of the field' look unneeded.

keyTerms.meaning: Isn't it all the more so? (a stronger-case argument)

steps.confusionAlert: Being 'cursed more' here means a longer pregnancy. The question only makes sense once you know tame animals already carry longer than wild ones.

phrases.english: If it was cursed more than the tame animals,
phrases.notes: 'It' is the snake. 'Cursed more' means it got a longer pregnancy than they did.

phrases.english: then more than the wild animals, isn't it all the more so?

steps.triggerLanguage: אִם מִבְּהֵמָה נִתְקַלְּלָה מֵחַיָּה לֹא כׇּל שֶׁכֵּן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the wording of the פסוק quoted in step 23.
steps.kashyaTarget: The phrase 'and more than all the beasts of the field' in the פסוק.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The shortest tame-animal pregnancy is already longer than the shortest wild-animal pregnancy, so mentioning the wild animals seems to add nothing.

steps.title: The extra words teach a ratio of one to seven
steps.stepSummary: The mention of wild animals teaches a comparison: tame animals were cursed more than wild animals by a ratio of one to seven.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, it comes to tell you: just as the tame animals were cursed more than the wild animals, one to seven...
steps.whatsHappening: רב יהודה continues his derivation and answers that the 'extra' words are there to teach a ratio. The sentence is only half finished here; the next steps complete it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק names both groups so we can compare them. The gap between wild and tame animals is a ratio of one to seven. The same ratio will then be used to work out the snake's pregnancy.

phrases.english: Rather, it comes to tell you:
just as the tame animals were cursed more than the wild animals,
one to seven,
phrases.notes: The tame animal's pregnancy is about seven times as long as the wild animal's.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 24.
steps.terutzResolutionType: The extra words are not repetition; they set up a ratio.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The words 'beasts of the field' seemed unneeded.
steps.terutzMaskana: They teach a one-to-seven ratio used to work out the snake's pregnancy.

steps.title: Which animals show the one-to-seven ratio?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא stops to ask which tame and wild animals show the one-to-seven ratio.
steps.simpleTranslation: And what is that?
steps.whatsHappening: A quick side question in the middle of the sentence: which animals are being compared? The answer comes right after.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ratio needs a real example to be useful. Without one, we could not apply it to the snake.

keyTerms.meaning: And what is it? (asking for the specific case)

phrases.english: And what is that?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for the specific example behind the ratio in step 25.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Which tame animal compared with which wild animal shows the one-to-seven ratio.

steps.title: The donkey compared with the cat
steps.stepSummary: The example is the חמור (donkey) compared with the חתול (cat).
steps.simpleTranslation: A donkey compared with a cat.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא names the two animals: the donkey, a tame animal, and the cat, a wild animal.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The donkey carries about twelve months, and the cat carries about 52 days. Seven times 52 is 364 days, which is almost exactly a year. That is the one-to-seven ratio.

phrases.english: A donkey compared with a cat,

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers step 26.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Donkey (about 12 months) compared with cat (about 52 days).

steps.title: So the snake carries for seven years
steps.stepSummary: Using the same ratio, the נחש's pregnancy is seven times the donkey's single year, which comes to seven years.
steps.simpleTranslation: So too, it (the snake) was cursed more than the tame animals, one to seven, which comes to seven years.
steps.whatsHappening: רב יהודה finishes the sentence. He applies the one-to-seven ratio to the snake and gets seven years, proving the ברייתא's number.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The donkey's one year (the longest pregnancy of the tame animals) times seven equals seven years for the snake. This completes רב יהודה's answer to the question in step 22, but the next steps challenge it.
steps.whatToRemember: The snake's seven-year pregnancy comes from the extra words 'beasts of the field' in its curse. They teach a one-to-seven ratio (donkey to cat), and applying it to the donkey's one year gives seven years for the snake.

phrases.english: so too it was cursed more than the tame animals,
phrases.notes: 'It' is the snake, compared with the donkey's one-year pregnancy.

phrases.english: one to seven,
which comes to seven years.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes the comparison begun in step 25, using the example from step 27.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: The snake's pregnancy is seven years: the donkey's one year times the one-to-seven ratio.

steps.title: Maybe the ratio is one to three instead
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא proposes a different reading of the פסוק: wild animals were cursed more than tame animals by a ratio of one to three years.
steps.simpleTranslation: Say instead: just as the wild animals were cursed more than the tame animals, by one year to three years…
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא opens a challenge to the seven-year conclusion by suggesting a different ratio. This is only the first half of the challenge; the full point comes in step 32.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 28 built seven years on a one-to-seven ratio. Here the גמרא says the פסוק might be pointing to a different comparison between wild and tame animals, a one-to-three ratio. If the starting ratio changes, the final number for the נחש changes too.

keyTerms.meaning: Say / maybe it means. A word that opens another way to read something.

steps.confusionAlert: Notice the direction has flipped. In step 25 the tame animal had the longer curse, but here the wild animal (the lion) carries longer than the tame one (the donkey).

phrases.english: Say [instead]:
just as the wild animal was cursed more than the tame animal,
one year to three years,

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the seven-year conclusion of step 28 by proposing a different base ratio.
steps.kashyaTarget: The one-to-seven ratio (donkey to cat) used in steps 25–28.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Nothing forces the one-to-seven pairing. A different pair of animals gives a one-to-three ratio, so the calculation could come out differently.

steps.title: Which animals have this one-to-three ratio?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא pauses inside the challenge to ask which animals show the one-to-three ratio.
steps.simpleTranslation: And which animals are those?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא stops in the middle of its challenge to ask for a real example of the one-to-three ratio. It is setting up the answer in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A ratio is only believable if it matches real animals. This is the same kind of pause the גמרא made in step 26 for the one-to-seven ratio.

keyTerms.meaning: What is it? A request to name the specific case.

phrases.english: And what is that?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: An interruption inside the challenge of step 29, asking for a concrete example.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Which pair of wild and tame animals has a one-to-three pregnancy ratio.

steps.title: The lion compared with the donkey
steps.stepSummary: The example is the ארי (lion), which carries for three years, compared with the חמור (donkey), which carries for one year.
steps.simpleTranslation: The lion compared with the donkey.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא names the animals: the lion and the donkey.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The donkey is the same tame animal used before, carrying one year. Pairing it with the lion (three years) instead of the cat gives a one-to-three ratio.

keyTerms.meaning: Lion, the wild animal here, which carries for three years

phrases.english: a lion compared to a donkey,

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 30.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The lion (three years) compared with the donkey (one year).

steps.title: Then the snake should carry for nine years
steps.stepSummary: Using the one-to-three ratio, the נחש is cursed three times more than the lion's three years, which makes nine years.
steps.simpleTranslation: So too, the snake was cursed more than the wild animal, by one to three years, which comes to nine years.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא finishes its challenge: with the lion's ratio, the נחש's pregnancy should be nine years, not seven.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Take the lion's three years and multiply by three, and you get nine. That contradicts the seven years from step 28, so the גמרא needs to explain why the one-to-seven reading is the right one.
steps.whatToRemember: Two readings now compete: donkey-to-cat (one to seven) gives the נחש seven years, while lion-to-donkey (one to three) gives nine years.

phrases.english: so too, he was cursed more than the wild animal
phrases.notes: "He" is the נחש, and the wild animal here is the lion.

phrases.english: one year to three years,
which makes it nine years.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes the challenge begun in step 29, now using the lion example from step 31.
steps.kashyaTarget: The conclusion of step 28 that the נחש carries for seven years.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Applying the lion's one-to-three ratio gives nine years, so the seven-year result is not the only possible reading of the פסוק.
